evidence_quotes.quote: O objetivo é avaliar como o PSA contribui para a conservação e melhoria da quantidade e qualidade da água em bacias hidrográficas. A metodologia do artigo combina revisão bibliográfica em direito da cidade, direito ambiental, governança e gestão hídrica, com análise de documentos e relatórios do projeto local.

Inspirada pelo Programa Produtor de Água da Agência Nacional de Águas (ANA) e por experiências internacionais, a Empresa Municipal de Água e Saneamento de Balneário Camboriú (EMASA) lançou o Produtor de Água do Rio Camboriú. Essa iniciativa visa garantir a conservação dos recursos hídricos na bacia do Rio Camboriú, incentivando proprietários rurais a adotarem práticas conservacionistas em suas propriedades por meio de apoio financeiro (EMASA, 2016).

O GG é encarregado de conduzir a vistoria em campo, conforme estabelecido na etapa 6, e de elaborar o parecer final sobre a elegibilidade do produtor rural para receber pagamentos por serviços ambientais, que corresponde à etapa 9.
A cidade de Balneário Camboriú incorporou os custos da conservação de água nas tarifas de água, após a experiência do projeto do Rio Camboriú.

A análise demonstrou que 81,25% dos contratos foram renovados, 55,6% das instituições parceiras participaram efetivamente das vistorias e 88,9% estão presentes nas reuniões do Grupo Gestor. Até 2017, foram restaurados 39,11 ha, o que representa 7,82% da meta estabelecida pelo projeto.

Em 2019, o Produtor de Água do Rio Camboriú contava com a participação de 26 produtores rurais que implementaram práticas para a recuperação de áreas degradadas, conservação dos remanescentes florestais nativos, manejo adequado do solo e preservação de estradas rurais. Totalizam-se 1.141,39 hectares de áreas conservadas e 70,68 hectares em processo de restauração. E ainda, 172 nascentes e 70,20 km de trechos de rios estão protegidos pelo projeto (EMASA, 2024.).

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although motivated by seasonal municipal water supply stress in Balneário Camboriú, the study examines upstream watershed and ecosystem conservation (Payment for Environmental Services to rural landowners to conserve/restore riparian vegetation and springs in the Camboriú River basin) rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes plain wording of Criterion 2 (yes), but fails narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (no). Under the plain broad wording, the paper examines legal, institutional, and governance frameworks for Payment for Environmental Services (State Law 15.133/2010, inter-institutional management by EMASA, ARESC, ANA, TNC, and the Grupo Gestor, landowner inspection/eligibility procedures, and a brief note that conservation costs were incorporated into water tariffs). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 is not met because the eligibility and inspection rules govern conservation payments to upstream rural landowners rather than household or community access to water or sanitation services, and the one-sentence mention of incorporating conservation costs into municipal water tariffs is unanalysed background on PES financing rather than an examination of tariff rules governing household service access or affordability. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because c1 and c4 are not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Unclear/borderline. The methodology combines bibliographic legal/policy review with descriptive analysis of project documents and secondary studies (citing monitoring totals from EMASA and Santos & Schwingel 2017, 2019), without primary data collection or original empirical evaluation of water supply impacts.
criterion_notes.c4: No. All reported metrics are upstream land-conservation and PES program-process outputs (26 participating rural landowners, 1,141.39 ha conserved, 39.11 ha restored by 2017 and 70.68 ha in restoration by 2019, 172 springs and 70.20 km of river protected, 81.25% contract renewal, partner attendance). No empirical outcome measuring household or community water access, connection, continuity, quantity delivered, affordability, or exclusion is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: No. While the upstream watershed case and participating rural landowners (26 properties) are described for conservation outputs, there is no identifiable household/community service-access population, service-access rule exposure, or empirical service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in Portuguese, which is eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Bibliographic legal/policy review and secondary document-based case study
population_and_sample: Camboriú River watershed (Santa Catarina, Brazil); 26 participating rural landowners/properties in the Rio Camboriú Water Producer Project (as of 2019)
exposure: Payment for Environmental Services (PSA) watershed conservation program (Projeto Produtor de Água do Rio Camboriú) providing financial and technical incentives to upstream rural landowners
outcome: Upstream watershed conservation and PES program implementation metrics (1,141.39 ha conserved, 39.11 ha restored by 2017 and 70.68 ha in restoration by 2019, 172 springs and 70.20 km of river protected, 81.25% contract renewal); no empirical household or community water service access outcomes reported
rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic — upstream watershed/ecosystem conservation unrelated to household or community service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7). This Portuguese-language article reviews legal and institutional aspects of Payment for Environmental Services (PSA) and presents a secondary document-based case study of the Rio Camboriú Water Producer Project (Projeto Produtor de Água) in Santa Catarina, Brazil. It fails c1 because it studies upstream riparian/spring conservation payments to rural landowners rather than household or community water or sanitation service access; fails c2 under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because the administrative/inspection rules govern conservation payments to rural landowners (and the single-sentence mention of incorporating conservation costs into water tariffs is unanalysed financing background rather than an examination of tariff rules governing household service access); and fails c4 because all reported data are land-restoration and PES contract metrics (hectares conserved/restored, springs protected, landowner participation) with no measured household or municipal water-access outcome. Even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for failing c1 and c4.
